OVERVIEW OF THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND The University had its beginning as the State Agricultural School chartered in 1888.
The federal Morrill Act of 1862 provided the framework within which the school became the land-grant institution of the State of Rhode Island (the “State”) and in 1892, the school became the Rhode Island College of Agricultural and Mechanic Arts.
The first class of 17 members was graduated two years l ater.

In 1909 the name of the College was changed to Rhode Island State College and the program of study was revised and expanded.
In 1951, the college became known as the University of Rhode Island by act of the State’s General Assembly.
The University of Rhode Island is the S tate’s flagship land and sea grant research institution, with a commitment to urban initiatives.
A student-centered research institution, URI actively partners with other organizations globally and locally to advance knowledge and t o develop informed residents and leaders.
URI is committed to high -quality education, community engagement, and solving the world’s most important challenges.
Situated on the traditional land and territories of the Narragansett Nation and the Niantic People, URI strives to create a diverse and inclusive environment for researchers, teachers, learners, and community members.
URI’s Strategic Plan, Focus URI 2023-2033, lays out the strategic vision for the University for the next decade, outlining four strategic priorities and the actions the University will take to achieve them:

A-3 Strategic Priority 1: Broaden the University’s impact through a reinvigorated commitment to its land- and sea-grant missions and the State of Rhode Island Strategic Priority 2: Enhance student achievement by cultivating an engaged and inclusive learning environment Strategic Priority 3: Foster an inclusive, people-centered culture Strategic Priority 4: Implement leading-edge administrative and financial systems and practices to power the University of the future The University’s main campus in Kingston, RI encompasses approximately 1,400 acres in Kingston, 30 miles south of Providence in the nor theastern metropolitan corridor between New York and Boston.
The 165-acre Narragansett Bay Campus (the “Bay Campus”), located six miles to the east overlooking the west passage of the Narragansett Bay, is home to the Graduate School of Oceanography , and the Ocean Engineering Department of the College of Engineering, and the College of Environment and Life Sciences.
In Providence, the University offers degree programs and non- credit courses and workshops in various locations.

In the western section of the State, 20 miles from Kingston, the 2,300 acres of woods, fields, streams and ponds on the W.
Alton Jones Campus are the site of research by various principal investigators.
The University offers degree programs through the doctoral level.
The University had a combined graduate, undergraduate and dual high school enrollment headcount of 14,452 students for the fall 2023 official reporting.
First year applications for fall 2023 were once again at record levels with 25,391 applications.
GOVERNANCE The Board of Governors for Higher Education became the governing body for the University in 1981, until the Board of Education assumed governance in January 2013.
In 2014, the Board of Education created two councils, including the Council on Postsecondary Education (the “Council”) which exercised oversight of the University, Rhode Island College (“RIC”), and the Community College of Rhode Island (“CCRI”).
On February 1, 2020, governance of the University was transferred to the newly constituted Board of Trustees for the University of Rhode Island (the “Board of Trustees” or the “URI Board”), whose purpose is the oversight of the University .

The Board of Education and the Council will continue to provide oversight for RIC and CCRI .
The URI Board assumed all the powers and duties with respect to the University formerly assigned to the Board of Education and the Council.
The State continues to oversee State funding of higher education, approve borrowing and drive education policy.
The University is held to meeting performance measures required by the State .
The new organizational structure for URI did not materially change the funding or financing arrangements of the State's three public higher education institutions, except in that the URI Board of Trustees has final approval of tuition and mandatory fee rates.
The new URI Board continues to share responsibility for its portion of previously issued bonds for the State’s colleges, which include debt issued by all three public higher institutions in the State: URI, Rhode Island College, and the Community College of Rhode Island.
The enabling legislation creating the Board of Trustees is codified in Rhode Island General Laws Title 16, Chapter 32.

A-4 The Trustees were originally appointed with staggered terms to ensure continuity on the Board.
On an annual basis, trustees are considered for appointment and reappointment by the Governor and are confirmed by the State legislature by the end of each legislative session, typically by June.
Three-year terms will again be staggered, as shown by the term expiration dates of those Trustees who have been reappointed to date.
The Faculty Senate was authorized in 1960 by the general faculty to conduct any business assigned to the faculty by law or by the Rhode Island Board of Educ ation/Council on Postsecondary Education and now by the Board of Trustees.

RESEARCH – GRANTS AND CONTRACTS In 2024, extramural grants and contracts to URI’s Division of Research and Economic Development totaled $145.9 M.
The activities supported by this funding are fundamental to URI’s mission as a RI’s flagship public research university.
The diverse and cutting -edge research conducted by URI faculty enhances academic programs and provides URI students with ample opportunities to participate in experiential, out- of-classroom educational experiences.
These opportunities range from laboratory -based research , international field work, to creative pursuits in our music and art studio.
Diverse funding sources f or grants and awards reflect the University’s growing standing as a significant catalyst for research and economic development in RI and nationally.
URI research powers foundational discoveries and sustains collaborative networks.
For example, URI is the longstanding home to the Rhode Island IDEA Network of Biomedical Research Excellence (RI -INBRE).

The overarching goal of (RI - INBRE) is to improve institutional capacity for biomedical research excellence and expand student experiential training opportunities in the State of Rhode Island.
The RI -INBRE network includes other publicly funded institutions of higher education in RI (Community College of Rhode Island, Rhode Island College) along with Brown University, Bryant University, Johnson and Wales University, Providence College, Roger Williams University and Salve Regina University.
URI is also the lead and coordinating institution for Rhode Island’s Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR) E -CORE program funded by the National Science Foundation.
The RI EPSCoR E -CORE Inclusive Network for Excellence in Science and Technology (RII-NEST) will strengthen research infrastructure and capacity in RI and position the state to sustain equitable, use-inspired research and societal and economic growth into the future .
The EPSCoR program also supports a state - wide network of mentored undergraduate research experiences including training in both field and laboratory-based research, data analytics, scientific presentations and manuscript writing.

The RII-NEST program brings together the Narragansett Indian Tribe, t he state’s public institutions of higher education (Community College of Rhode Island, Rhode Island College) and private institutions (Brown University, The Rhode Island School of Design and Roger Williams University).
Additionally, the University enhances its land- and sea-grant research mission by acquiring federal funding aimed at solving problems addressing crucial societal and environmental concerns for our communities.
For example, URI researchers are addressing problems of “forever chemicals” poly - and perfluoroalkyl substances-PFAS in the environment in the Sources, Transport, Exposure and Effects of PFAS (STEEP) project.
With funding from the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS), STEEP researchers have been elucidating en vironmental and human health impacts of PFAS exposure and disseminating knowledge to prevent future contamination.
URI’s broad research portfolio is woven into the University’s teaching, mentorship, and community life in a myriad of ways.

For example, the annual URI Honors Colloquium has a topical focus that often draws on our research (e.g., ocean health, food security).
Th e URI Honors Colloquium is open to both the campus community and the public and is very well-attended and impactful.
There are numerous seminars, colloquia, invited lectures, exhibits, plays and performances each week – all stemming from the University’s emphasis on its research programs – that contribute deeply to both the education of the University’s students and to the broader community that URI serves.

The College of Pharmacy offers the six-year Doctor of Pharmacy degree for students seeking admission at the undergraduate level.

Special Academic Opportunities Honors Program The Universit y Honors Program provides students the opportunity to take dynamic, interdisciplinary courses and engage in original research alongside faculty who are leaders in their fields in the sciences, business, and humanities.
The program offers motivated students enrichment opportunities through smaller class sizes, individualized advising and mentoring, and participation in a research or creative project working under the guidance of a faculty mentor.
The program also sponsors a colloquium each year that brings together distinguished national and international experts on contemporary topics who share their thoughts and work with students and the wider community.
National Student Exchange Program National Student Exchange (“NSE”) inspires academic enrichment, pe rsonal exploration, and student development by facilitating accessible collegiate study away among member colleges and universities throughout the United States, Canada, Guam, Puerto Rico and U.S Virgin Islands.
With 173 member institutions, students have access to many options.
Some NSE campuses offer unique opportunities beyond traditional classroom learning.

A-12 Center for Career and Experiential Education The University of Rhode Island’s Center for Career and Experiential Education (“CCEE”) engages undergraduate students and alumni in a personal and professional educational experience, from admission through employment.
The Center values its relationships with local and national employer partners and seeks to find innovative ways to connect students, alumni, faculty, and employ ers in the career education and development process.
The team of Career Education Specialists (“CES”) offer individual and group professional development sessions and on- line modules for students and alumni.
The topics include self - assessments to discover one’s strengths, job and internship searching, networking and brand development strategies, resume and cover letter development, salary negotiation, interviewing skills, and major to career industry clusters.
The highest impact practice involves engaging in opportunities and courses which include relevant connections between coursework, the community and the workforce.

CCEE offers service learning and internship courses to explore a variety of occupations and gain practical experience through an internship or civic engagement.
The Employer Relations team develops relationships with local and national employers to connect students and alumni with their desired industries.
This is done through the Rhody Alumni Mentoring (“RAM”) program, career and volunteer fa irs, networking events, on -campus interviewing, job, internship and volunteer posting, and professional development week.
Rhode Island Inter-institutional Exchange Full-time students matriculated at one of the public institutions of higher education in Rhode Island may enroll for a maximum of eight credits of their full-time schedule per semester for study at one of the other public institutions at no additional expe nse.
Each institution will determine and maintain the integrity of the degree to be awarded.
The University has a robust system of transfer and prior-approved courses, along with articulation agreements with the Community College of Rhode Island and other feeder institutions.

Study Abroad The Office of International Education & National Student Exchange promotes the internationalization of education and building of students’ cross -cultural global skills through educational opportunities in a variety of global environments and institutional linkages.
While international education was curtailed in the spring of academic year 2020 and fall and spring of academic year 2021 due to the pandemic, the University has resumed international education and exchanges for the 2022-2023 year.
In a normal year the University offers more than 800 study abroad options in more than 60 countries worldwide through URI sponsored programs and global affiliations; off -campus credit bearing experiences exist for students in all aca demic disciplines.
The wide array of learning experiences managed by the office aim to support the institutional objective of expanding the global learning opportunities available to the student body and promoting the institutional objective of ensuring that all students are exposed to global perspectives and build global competency skills.
Options beyond traditional classroom learning are available.

These include international internships, research, field study, virtual engagements and other experiential learning opportunities such as ship-based research voyages.
Semester and short-term programs during the Winter J-Term session, Spring Break, and Summer Session programs are available each academic year.
The office also provides comprehensive advising and programming services – from program selection to predeparture preparation and reentry programming – to support student success in all aspects of the education abroad process and context.
In a concerted effort to increase accessibility and affordability, student assistance in securing local and national scholarship awards is provided and developing quality cost-effective study options is given precedence.
Summer Sessions The University provides a full range of undergraduate and graduate course offerings on line and offers the opportunity to attend two five-week in-person sessions and a ten week in -person session on the Kingston

A-13 campus.
Courses begin immediately after Commencement and are offered online, during day and evenings.
Summer intensives are offered at varying dates in the alternate session, and several special programs, including study in foreign countries, internships, and clinical placements, are available.
Winter J-Term Session URI offers a “J-Term”, which is an academic mini-semester over winter session (the approximately three- week period between January 2 and the day before the spring semester begins) that consists of credit-bearing courses that offer new value-added experiences for students not possible during standard semesters and/or allow students to catch up or retake certain courses.
Over 1800 students take part in this mini -term each year.
Military Science and Leadership (Army Reserve Officers’ Training Corps or “Army ROTC”) Military Science and Leadership is one of the nation’s top leadership programs.
Army ROTC is an elective curriculum that students take along with their required college classes.
The program provides students with tools, training, and experience to help the m succeed in any competitive environment.

Army ROTC also offers students the opportunity to earn two- , three-, and four -year scholarships covering full tuition and fees, book money, and a monthly allowance.
Military Science and Leadership is an elective course of study and students can participate during their freshman and sophomore years without any obligation to join the Army.
Marine and Environment-Related Programs Outstanding scholarship in marine science and oceanography at the University dates to the mid-1930s.
Over the past three decades, this strong emphasis on marine studies has extended to environmental topics, developing into an array of undergraduate programs in the natural, physical, and social sciences.

There are more than two dozen majors wi th a marine or environmental focus offered by URI’s colleges, including landscape architecture, physics and physical oceanography, ocean engineering, civil engineering, aquaculture and fishery technology, biological sciences, cell and molecular biology, environmental and natural resource economics, environmental science and management, geology and geological oceanography, marine affairs, marine biology, plant science, sustainable agriculture and food systems, and wildlife and conservation biology.
Several o f the majors are offered jointly with the Graduate School of Oceanography.
Undergraduates are encouraged to explore opportunities at the Narragansett Bay Campus for active participation in the oceanographic sciences.
Juniors and seniors may spend an entire semester at the University’s Bay Campus pursuing their individual marine interests, for which they receive full academic credit.
They work as part of a research team in the laboratory and in the field under the direct guidance of the Graduate School of Oceanography faculty.

Center for Student Leadership Development To enhance the mission of the University of Rhode Island, the Center for Student Leadership Development aims to provide developmental opportunities for all students to become informed, inclusive, effective, and ethical leaders in the global marketplace through the implementation of learner -centered academic, experiential, and co-curricular programming.
In addition, the Center engages in research, assessment, and advancement in order to positively impact the expanding field of leadership studies.
URI offers a minor in Leadership Studies that is customized for each student.
The program uses a cross-disciplinary approach to leadership education designed to complement a student’s academic studies.
All courses utilize a variety of teaching methods but ultimately include some form of experiential learning, practical application, and reflective learning.
LIBRARIES The University libraries include the Robert L.
Carothers Library and Learning Commons (Ki ngston Campus) and the Claiborne Pell Marine Science Library ( Narragansett Bay Campus).

A-14 libraries hold more than 1.3 million bound volumes, 750,000 government publications, 30,000 print journals as well as provide online access to more than 169,000 full text journals, 1,750,361 e-books, and over 300 online databases.

The National Sea Grant Depository was recently closed, and the University Libraries worked with NOAA to ensure that physical research materials were preserved and distributed to interested regional institutions nationwide.

The University Libraries has also been designated a preservation steward for all NOAA publications.
Staffed by 37 faculty and staff, the University Libraries offer a range of library services and spaces to complement the teaching, learning, and research mission of URI.
Library faculty lead sections of undergraduate information literacy courses, helping students fulfill core student learning outcomes.
Library staff ensure the accessibility of collections and study spaces to the University Community 99.5 hours per week during regular semesters, and a portion of the Carothers Library is open to support student learning 24/7.
Technical Services faculty and staff ensure the discoverability of and access to books, articles, and other essential research materials through materials acquisition, metadata creation and database maintenance.
Public Services faculty provide information research consultations, programmatic instruction, and point-of-need support for researchers of all levels at the Research Help Desk.

Collaborating with offices and colleges across campus, the Library Innovation Labs consisting of a Makerspace, XR Lab, and AV Lab offer access to and assistance with advanced technologies, while the Launch Lab highlights solution - and entrepreneurship-focused learning.
Recently, the Knit/We ar Technology Lab, a collaboration with the Colleges of Engineering and Business, has been established.
The Library also hosts URI’s Department of Information Technology Services (ITS) Service Desk, ITS’s Teaching and Learning Services, the Academic Innov ation Center, the University’s Active Learning Classroom, the Artificial Intelligence Lab, and functions of the Academic Enhancement Center.

The BLC focuses on providing high- quality and cost-effective sharing of print, digital and electronic content across member libraries, and acts as an incubator for initiatives relevant to academic and research libraries in the 21st century.

Tenure at the University provides for continuing academic appointment which may not be terminated, unless by jus t cause.

Employee Relations The University considers its relations with its faculty and staff to be good.
Fringe benefits include disability insurance, group life insurance, health insurance, dental insurance, retirement plans and a tuition remission program.
Approximately 30% of the University’s employees participate in the State’s employee defined benefit retirement system.
This participation includes classified and some non- classified employees.

In November 2011, the Rhode Island General Assembly enacted comprehensive pension refor m legislation which included implementing a supplemental defined contribution plan and other benefit and eligibility changes including suspending Cost of Living Adjustments.
The majority of faculty and non-classified staff participate in the Council on Postsecondary Education’s (the “Council’s”) defined contribution retirement plan 403 (b), in which the University continues to participate under the Board of Trustees as provided for in the Board’s enabling legislation.
The employee and the University make contributions to the 403(b) plan each pay period and the contributions are remitted directly to the plan(s).
There is no outstanding unfunded liability related to the Council’s retirement plans.
Concurrent active participation in both the State Retirement Plan and the Council’s plan is prohibited by law.

Academic Enhancement Center The Academic Enhancement Center (“AEC”) supports student learning and academic success through scaffolding student engagement with course content, helpi ng with the development of metacognitive strategies and skills, critical thinking, writing, time management, and test taking skills.
AEC programs are primarily peer-to-peer, enabling the Center to support the development of collaborative learning skills fo r all students, as well as teaching and leadership skills for student staff.

The AEC offers unique resources including three forms of tutoring in the STEM disciplines; an Academic Skills Development programming, including UCS 160; and the Writing Center for helping students at all levels of writing skills development.
The mission of the Academic Enhancement Center is to help students invest in their academic success.
The AEC learning support programs and services empower students to become more skillful and successful.
The AEC is committed to responding to student needs, collaborating with faculty and providing professional development for the student staff with the goal of enhancing student learning.

COMMUNITY, EQUITY AND DIVERSITY The Office of Community, Equity and Diversity leads institution- wide initiatives to anchor inclusion in every aspect of the University of Rhode Island’s community and operations.
The Office strives to advance inclusive excellence through impacting culture and climate by creating a welcoming community where each member can learn, work, and thrive; hosting communities of practice that foster cultural competence and model constructive dialogue a cross difference; incentivizing inclusivity in scholarship, research, pedagogy, and practices; incorporating inclusion in University policies and procedures by identifying and removing artificial barriers that impede the land grant mission and mandate to s upport all learners; and, iterating through coordinated and ongoing institution-wide assessment.

In addition, the Office of Community, Equity and Diversity oversees four centers that promote diversity, equity and inclusion: Women’s Center The URI Women’s Center partners with others in the URI community to provide an empowering space which promotes social justice for every member of the community, regardless of gender, gender identity, body, ability, sexual orientation, race, spirituality, and ethnicity.
C ommunity members are encouraged to

A-23 engage and foster continual dialogue on gender and issues that disproportionately affect woman-identified persons and their allies.
By developing, supporting and advocating for woman-identified persons’ abilities, talents, values and diverse identities, the URI Women’s Center supports all University students, faculty and staff in expanding their positive potential, agency and life experience.
Multicultural Student Services Center The URI Multicultural Student Services Center is dedicated to developing a supportive and inclusive campus culture across the boundaries of culture, identity, and discipline.
Celebrating unity in diversity, the Multicultural Center invites all students, fa culty, staff, administrators, alumni, and other friends to join in its work in creating a community of learners within and beyond URI.
The URI Multicultural Center collaboratively provides programs and resources that engage, connect and support the URI com munity in becoming just and culturally competent global citizens.
It also houses The Center for Nonviolence and Peace which promotes and studies approaches to addressing conflict through nonviolence.

Gender and Sexuality Center The URI Gender and Sexuali ty Center encourages students, faculty, and staff to explore and affirm their multiple and intersecting identities, especially surrounding gender and sexuality.
Through education, advocacy, and community- building, the Gender and Sexuality Center strives to cultivate an inclusive campus culture that celebrates all genders and sexual identities.
The Center provides intersectional programming and collaborates with student leaders and campus partners to strengthen community and foster belonging, all while nurtu ring a student-centered environment that supports academic and personal growth.
Center for Military and Veteran Education The Center for Military and Veteran Education serves and supports prior, present, and future military - connected students, faculty, an d staff as they further their educational and professional objectives.
The Center assists in the transition from military life into student life and beyond and helps veterans connect with the resources and networks of support available to them at URI and within the local community.

STUDENT SERVICES Auxiliary Services Auxiliary services consist of housing, dining, student union, health center and the campus store, which depend on restricted fees and related revenues derived from student clients.
These operations are required by State law to be fully self-supporting.
Undergraduate Housing On-campus residence halls are available to eligible students during the regular academic year and winter inter-session, with additional availability offered provided during the summer.
The University offers a variety of living accommodations with 27 residence halls and two apartment complexes.
The residence halls include 22 traditional residence halls, of which fourteen primarily house first year resident Living and Learning Communities, and three undergraduate apartment -style facilities, including the new Brookside apartment-style residence hall completed in January 2020.
There are also two International Engineering Program Houses.
First year students are strongly encouraged to live on campus other than in exceptional circumstances; in the fall of 2024 approximately 88% of URI first year students live in residence halls.

In the fall 202 4 semester, 579 University students reside in the fraternity/sorority system which sponsors 16 sororities and fraternities (the “Greek” houses) located on university land but not owned or operated by the University.
The staff of the Office of Greek Life in the Dean of Students Office advises these groups.
The Greek houses

A-24 promote scholarship, citizenship and small group living.
Purchasing and business management for these houses is provided by a private non-profit corporation controlled by the fraternity and sorority members.
In addition, students occupi ed two specialty houses for Engineering Students.
Another choice available to students is living "down the line" in rented rooms or houses near the University in the ocean- side resort areas.
For the fall 2024 semester, 5,325 undergraduates were resident i n on -campus (HRL) facilities on the Kingston campus.
Approximately 49% of URI undergraduate residents were first year students.
In fall 2024 approximately 60% of undergraduates lived off campus in nearby communities or commuted from home.
Graduate Housing On-campus apartments are available primarily for graduate students.
These apartments are available year- round.
Many graduate students also live off-campus in the local community.
Dining Centers Dining Services operates two all -you-care to eat fac ilities along with several retail locations across the Kingston Campus.
Additionally, they manage a convenience store in the residential complex as well as a production bakery and warehouse facility.

Students who live on campus in University residence hall s are required to purchase a University meal plan.
Dining works to provide locally sourced ingredients to provide a diverse offering while focusing on sustainability efforts.
Student Support Services Center for Career and Experiential Education.
The CCEE engages undergraduate students and alumni in a high quality personal and professional educational experience, from admission through employment.
The University has relationships with local and national employer partners and seeks to find innovative ways to connect students, alumni, faculty, and employers in the career education and development process.
Counseling Services.
The Counseling Center is staffed by licensed mental health counselors, psychologists, and social workers.
The Center offers indi vidual counseling and a variety of skill -building and support groups to help undergraduate and graduate students achieve their academic and life goals.

The Counseling Center provides assistance to students in areas such as adjusting to college life, coping with stress, building satisfying relationships, planning for the future, and coping with anxiety depression, substance use, or other mental health challenges.
The University partners with Telus Health to provide free, confidential, emotional health and wellbeing support, including access to clinicians 24/7 virtually, by phone or chat.
University Chaplains.
The University chaplains are active in providing religious services and in counseling, advising campus gro ups, teaching, and programming.
Faith groups include Buddhism, Catholic Center, Chabad, Congregational/UCC, Episcopal Ministry, Jewish Center, Muslim Center, Rhody Christ ian Fellowship, Sojourn Collegiate Ministry, Unitarian Universalist, and United Method ist.;.
The chaplains work together to foster dialogue, understanding, and respect among people of different faiths and traditions.
Memorial Union.
The center for campus programs and activities, the Memorial Union houses a wide variety of education, social and cultural services and facilities for undergraduate and graduate students.

These include the Student Entertainment Committee and Student Senate, many student organization offices, the Center for Student Leadership Development (an academic piece that offers a minor as well as peer education opportunities), staff that assist with room scheduling and an information desk.
Student Involvement staff are available to student leaders to provide advising and education in addition to assisting with the planning for their student organization’s events.

A-25 Health Services.
University Health Services provides primary ambulatory care to students.
Nurse practitioners and physicians see students by appointment Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. as well as Saturday and Sundays and most holidays from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Health Services provides laboratory, radiology, and pharmacy services for URI students.
Specialists in gynecology and psychiatry hold regular clinics at the Potter Building.
Health Promotion provides education to students on health and wellness issues that support student success while in college and throughout their lifetime.
Violence Prevention and Advocacy Services are a part of the Health Services providing awareness, education, and support f or survivors of sexual violence and Alcohol and other Drug Education provide comprehensive education, training and support on substance use and prevention.
A travel/immunization clinic administers vaccines available from the pharmacy.
Care provided at Health Services is billed to insurance companies.
The Dean of Students Office.
Staff provides a range of services for students, staff, and faculty focused on student success.

These services include Disability, Access, Inclusion Services for Students, Outreach and Intervention, the Office of Community Standards, Greek Life, and the Office of Commuter Affairs.
The Dean of Students is responsible for leading the university -wide Behavior Intervention Team and the Assistant Director of Outreach and Interven tion leads the Students of Concern Team.
Staff frequently provide training to faculty and are available for consultation.
Talent Development.
Talent Development recruits and serves Rhode Island high school graduates with college potential who come from historically disadvantaged backgrounds, a majority of whom are Scholars of color.
Talent Development enrolls approximately 1,100 students annually and its mission is grounded in the University’s mission of enriching students' lives through its land, sea and urban grant traditions. (See “Talent Development” under “Access and Affordability”).
INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY SERVICES The University’s Information Technology Services organization (“ITS”) provides leadership and strategic direction for technology and ente rprise systems that support the University of Rhode Island community.

ITS supports key systems used every day, including the Learning Management System for online classes, Enterprise Resource Planning systems for student records, HR, and finances, and the Help Desk, which provides technical support to the entire URI community.
ITS also manages the University's high -speed internet network, which links URI’s campuses to each other and to the wider world through a secure, multi- gigabit fiber-optic connection.
With growing demand for advanced technology in classrooms and research, ITS is strengthening its support for artificial intelligence, machine learning, and high -performance computing.
These advancements position URI as a leader in research and discovery.
F aculty and students use AI to create predictive healthcare models, develop early disease detection tools, and analyze large datasets to support public health and environmental sustainability.
High-performance computing drives major research in climate modeling, fisheries science, and coastal resilience, which are critical to Rhode Island’s future.
Enhanced computational resources enable faster simulations, large-scale data analysis, and breakthroughs in complex scientific challenges.

These tools increase UR I’s competitiveness for research grants from agencies like the National Science Foundation and National Institutes of Health.
They support faculty -driven research on national priorities and provide students with experience in cutting- edge technologies.
Students trained in AI and high - performance computing are well -positioned for careers in data science, engineering, and emerging technology fields.
Cybersecurity is a growing challenge for all institutions, and URI is no exception.
To protect sensitive information, ITS has strengthened its security systems.
This includes requiring multi-factor authentication

A-26 for most University systems, upgrading network security to prevent unauthorized access, and rebuilding URI's disaster recovery system to protect against ransomware attacks.
By supporting student learning, research, and day-to-day operations, ITS ensures that URI stays connected, secure, and ready for the future.
Strategic investments in areas like online learning, campus Wi-Fi, research tools, and cybersecurity help ensure that students and faculty have the resources they need to succeed.
FACILITIES The University’s current physical plant of 5. 7 million square feet across four campuses consists of 3 22 buildings (including leased buildings) including 24 residence halls, plus three apartment complexes and two dining centers, as well as the Memorial Union’s Ram’s Den.
Throughout its nearly continuous building program, the University has been successful in obtaining public financial support through the approval of bonds of the State issued for the benefit of the University for both renovation of older buildings and the construction of new buildings.

Over the last ten years, the University has completed more than $ 550 million in new construction and renovation an d rehabilitation of existing structures.
Recent Completed Construction and Major Renovations: 2013 to 2024 Robert J.
Higgins Welcome Center.
September 26, 2018 marked the official opening of the $8.2 million Robert J.
Higgins Welcome Center, funded by generous donors and one -time University funding sources.
Located on a prominent site on Upper College Road, this new state of the art building is an important tool for continuing the growth in applications which has enabled the University to increase enrollment significantly over the last ten years in the face of declining numbers of high school graduates nationally and regionally, while simultaneously increasing bo th the quality of the student body and its diversity.
The Higgins Welcome Center showcases URI students and their successes and enhances that all-important first impression for prospective students and families upon arrival at the Kingston Campus.
